title: “OBEY THE GOVERNMENT”—EVEN WHEN IT TELLS YOU TO DISOBEY GOD? THE TERRIFYING MISUSE OF ROMANS 13
paragraphs: “OBEY THE GOVERNMENT”—EVEN WHEN IT TELLS YOU TO DISOBEY GOD? THE TERRIFYING MISUSE OF ROMANS 13

One of the Bible’s most quoted commands about government has also become one of its most misunderstood. But what happens when obedience to earthly authority demands betrayal of the King of kings? The answer could change how you understand submission, courage, persecution, and what it truly means to follow Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing in a courtroom.
Your hands are trembling. Your family is waiting outside. The judge looks directly at you and gives you one final opportunity to walk away.
All you have to do is deny Jesus.
Just a few words.
No more prison. No more threats. No more uncertainty about whether you will see your children again.
Then someone standing beside you opens a Bible and whispers:
“Romans 13 says you must obey the governing authorities.”
And suddenly, the question becomes unbearable.
If God commands Christians to submit to government, would refusing that judge mean disobeying God Himself?
Would faithfulness to Jesus actually require denying Jesus?
Read that question again.

Because somewhere between a government demanding obedience and a believer trying to remain faithful, a Scripture written to teach Christians how to live responsibly under civil authority can be twisted into something the apostle Paul never intended.
And the consequences are not merely theological.
They can reach into churches, families, courtrooms, prison cells, and the conscience of an ordinary Christian who simply wants to do what is right before God.
Here is the truth we must confront.
Romans 13 commands Christians to submit to governing authorities. It does not command Christians to commit sin whenever governing authorities demand it.
And if we misunderstand that distinction, we can mistake surrendering our conscience for surrendering our lives to Christ.
But before we condemn those who misuse Romans 13, we need to ask a more uncomfortable question.
Have we actually read what Paul wrote?
Not merely the verse someone quoted during an argument.
Not the sentence lifted from its context to defend a politician, silence a Christian, or justify rebellion.
The actual words.
The actual context.
The actual Gospel that shaped the man who wrote them.
Because the truth is more demanding than either blind obedience or reckless defiance.
And it begins with a sentence that leaves no room for casually dismissing civil authority.
“Let every soul be in subjection to the higher powers: for there is no power but of God; and the powers that be are ordained of God.”
— Romans 13:1, American Standard Version (1901)
Paul's original Greek begins:
Πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις ὑποτασσέσθω.
Pasa psychē exousiais hyperechousais hypotassesthō.
A careful rendering is:
“Let every person be subject to the governing authorities.”
Notice the word ὑποτασσέσθω (hypotassesthō).
It comes from hypotassō, meaning to place oneself under an established order or to be subject to authority.
Paul is not encouraging Christians to treat government as irrelevant.
He is commanding a genuine posture of submission.
That matters.
Christians are not automatically more spiritual because they distrust officials, ignore laws, refuse taxes, or oppose every government decision they dislike.
A rebellious spirit does not become holy simply because someone attaches a Bible verse to it.
But neither does a government become morally infallible simply because God permits it to exercise authority.
That is where the deeper question begins.
Paul says governing authority exists under God's sovereign ordering.
He does not say that every decision made by every ruler expresses God's moral approval.
Those are radically different claims.
God can establish the place of civil government in human society without approving the corruption, cruelty, injustice, or idolatry of particular rulers.
The same Bible that commands respect for governing authority also records God confronting kings, judging nations, exposing oppression, and condemning leaders who abuse their power.
God is sovereign over earthly authority.
Earthly authority is not sovereign over God.
And that distinction becomes impossible to ignore when we remember the world in which Paul wrote.
He was not writing from the comfort of a modern democracy with constitutional protections, elections, and broad guarantees of religious freedom.
He was writing to Christians in Rome, the center of an empire ruled by Caesar.
The emperor at the time was Nero.

The early years of Nero's reign preceded the notorious persecution of Christians associated with the aftermath of Rome's great fire in AD 64. Paul was therefore not writing Romans 13 in response to that later persecution. Nevertheless, his readers lived under an imperial system in which political authority was concentrated in rulers who were neither Christian nor morally accountable to Scripture.
Paul knew what unjust power looked like.
And yet he commanded submission.
Why?
Because the Christian life is not a license for disorder.
Because God cares about justice, peace, responsibility, and the protection of human society.
Because the Gospel does not turn every personal grievance into a divine mandate for resistance.
And because the Christian's freedom in Christ must never become an excuse to harm neighbors or despise legitimate authority.
But here is something we cannot afford to overlook.
The same Paul who wrote Romans 13 also endured punishment, imprisonment, and opposition for proclaiming Jesus Christ.
He did not understand submission as permission for the state to silence the Gospel.
He did not believe civil authority could cancel his commission from Christ.
He respected the proper place of government while continuing to obey the Lord who stood above every earthly throne.
And this is where Scripture itself provides the clearest answer.
Picture another courtroom.
Two apostles are standing before religious authorities who have already warned them to stop preaching.
They are not accused of stealing.
They are not plotting violence.
They are not trying to seize political power.
They are preaching Jesus Christ.
And the authorities have commanded them to stop.
Peter and the other apostles respond:
“We must obey God rather than men.”
— Acts 5:29, American Standard Version (1901)
The original Greek is unmistakable:
Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.
Peitharchein dei theō mallon ē anthrōpois.
“We must obey God rather than human beings.”
The word μᾶλλον (mallon) expresses the priority: God rather than people when their demands conflict.
This was not a rejection of all human authority.
It was a declaration that human authority has limits.

Although Acts 5 concerns religious authorities rather than a civil governor, it establishes a principle that applies whenever any human authority commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands.
And Scripture does not leave that principle standing alone.
Remember the three Hebrew men standing before King Nebuchadnezzar.
Shadrach.
Meshach.
Abednego.
The king had commanded worship before a golden image.
The consequences of refusal were terrifying.
A blazing furnace.
Public humiliation.
Death.
They were not given a comfortable option.
They could bow and live, or refuse and face the fire.
Their answer remains one of the most courageous confessions recorded in Scripture.

Daniel 3:17–18, in the Aramaic portion of the book of Daniel, records their confidence that God was able to deliver them, while also declaring that even if He did not, they would not serve the king's gods or worship his image.
The words לָא־פָלְחִין (lāʾ pālḥîn) express their refusal to serve those gods.
They did not deny the king's political position.
They denied his right to command idolatry.
And there is something breathtaking about their faith.
They did not demand that God rescue them before they would obey Him.
They chose obedience even without a guarantee of deliverance.
That is not rebellion for rebellion's sake.
That is worship.
And if we are going to interpret Romans 13 faithfully, we must interpret it alongside Daniel 3.
Alongside the Hebrew midwives in Exodus 1, who feared God and refused Pharaoh's murderous command.
Alongside Daniel 6, where Daniel continued praying to God despite a royal decree designed to prohibit it.
Alongside Acts 4 and 5, where the apostles refused to abandon their witness to Christ.
And alongside Revelation 13, where earthly political power is portrayed as demanding worship and allegiance that belong to God alone.
Think about that last passage.
Romans 13 teaches that governing authority has a God-given role.
Revelation 13 warns that political power can become monstrous when it demands what belongs to God.
These passages are not enemies.
They reveal two truths that must be held together.
Government deserves proper submission because its legitimate authority is accountable to God. Government must never receive worship because only God is worthy of absolute allegiance.
This is not a contradiction.
It is a boundary.
And it is a boundary written into the words of Jesus Himself.
When His opponents tried to trap Him with a question about paying taxes to Caesar, Jesus asked whose image appeared on the coin.
Then He said:
“Render therefore unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.”
— Matthew 22:21, American Standard Version (1901)
Do not miss the brilliance of His answer.
Jesus acknowledged a legitimate claim of civil government.
But He also distinguished that claim from what belongs to God.
Caesar may receive what is properly Caesar's.
He may not receive what belongs to the Creator.
Taxes may belong to the state.
Worship belongs to God.
Civil duties may be owed to rulers.
Ultimate allegiance belongs to Jesus Christ.
Your conscience must be formed by God's Word, not surrendered unconditionally to the commands of human power.
And your soul is not Caesar's property.
Now let us return to Romans 13, because there is another detail that changes how we understand the passage.
Paul does not merely say that authorities possess power.
He describes the purpose of that authority.
“For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil.”
— Romans 13:3, American Standard Version (1901)
Then he calls the ruler God's servant for good in Romans 13:4.
The Greek expression is:
θεοῦ γὰρ διάκονός ἐστιν σοὶ εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν.
Theou gar diakonos estin soi eis to agathon.
“For he is God's servant to you for good.”
The word διάκονος (diakonos) means servant or minister.
The ruler is not described as a god.
He is described as a servant.
And a servant is accountable to the One he serves.
Paul is explaining the proper function of civil authority: restraining wrongdoing and supporting what is good.
We should be careful here.

Romans 13 does not explicitly provide a complete theory of civil disobedience or a detailed legal procedure for resisting unjust rulers. Christians have differed over how its principles apply to particular governments, forms of resistance, and political systems.
But the wider witness of Scripture makes one point clear: an official's command does not turn an evil action into a righteous one.
When a ruler protects the vulnerable, punishes wrongdoing justly, and maintains public order, that ruler is acting consistently with the purpose Paul describes.
When a ruler commands idolatry, persecution, or murder, the ruler is acting contrary to God's moral will.
And the Christian must distinguish between respecting the office and endorsing every action of the person occupying it.
This matters because there are two dangerous ways to misuse Romans 13.
The first is to make government absolute.
To tell Christians they must obey every command, even if it requires sin.
To demand silence when authorities prohibit the faithful proclamation of Christ.
To excuse cruelty because someone powerful signed a decree.
To treat disagreement with a leader as rebellion against God Himself.
That is not biblical submission.
That is the elevation of human authority beyond its rightful place.
But the second danger is just as real.
It is using the limits of governmental authority as an excuse for pride, contempt, lawlessness, or political fanaticism.
It is declaring every inconvenient regulation an attack on Christianity.
It is refusing ordinary civic responsibilities because we dislike those in office.
It is treating political opponents as enemies to be hated rather than neighbors to be loved.
It is confusing personal preference with divine command.
And it is imagining that because we claim to defend God, every angry reaction must be justified.
Beloved, not every law you dislike violates Scripture.
Not every government policy you oppose is persecution.
Not every political defeat is a spiritual attack.
And not every act of resistance is obedience to Jesus.
Sometimes faithfulness requires standing firm against an unjust command.
Sometimes faithfulness requires paying the tax, following the law, honoring the official, and refusing to let resentment rule your heart.
Romans 13:6–7 specifically addresses paying taxes and giving what is owed, including respect and honor.
That part of the passage is often forgotten by people who enjoy quoting only the verses that support their preferred political position.
But Paul does not allow us to edit Scripture to fit our anger.
And neither does Jesus.
The chapter immediately before Romans 13 gives us a remarkable picture of how Christians should live.
Romans 12 calls believers to bless persecutors, refuse vengeance, pursue peace where possible, and overcome evil with good.
Then Romans 13 speaks about submission to governing authorities.
The chapter numbers were added long after Paul wrote the letter.
His argument flows continuously.
That means Romans 13 should not be separated from the command to overcome evil with good.
Christian resistance, when conscience genuinely requires it, must still be shaped by the character of Christ.
It must not become an excuse for revenge.
It must not be driven by hatred.
It must not confuse cruelty with courage.
And it must not pretend that doing something in Jesus' name automatically makes it righteous.
There may be times when believers must respectfully refuse an unlawful-in-God's-sight demand, accept the consequences, seek lawful remedies, appeal unjust decisions, or protect those being harmed.
But even then, our conduct must reflect the Lord we claim to serve.
Because the Christian is not called merely to win against earthly power. The Christian is called to remain faithful to Christ.
And that brings us to the most searching part of this entire conversation.
What happens when obeying Jesus costs us something?
Not in theory.
Not in a comment section.
Not in a debate where everyone goes home comfortable.
But in real life.
What happens when telling the truth threatens your career?
When refusing corruption costs you an opportunity?
When defending someone vulnerable makes powerful people angry?
When obedience to Christ means losing approval, security, or freedom?
What happens when compromise would make your life easier?
It is one thing to announce that we would stand with Daniel before the lions.
It is another thing to stand for truth when our own comfort is on the line.
It is easy to admire the apostles for saying they must obey God rather than men.
It is harder to obey God when doing so may cost us something we desperately want to keep.
And perhaps that is why this passage should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Because some of us have spent so much time asking whether Christians should obey the government that we have neglected a more personal question.
Are we obeying Jesus in the places where no government is forcing us to do anything?
We argue about religious freedom while refusing to forgive someone who wounded us.
We defend biblical morality publicly while hiding dishonesty privately.
We demand righteous leaders while excusing pride, bitterness, and corruption in ourselves.
We speak passionately about God's authority over nations while resisting His authority over our own desires.
And suddenly Romans 13 is no longer merely about presidents, kings, judges, or lawmakers.
It is about lordship.
Who actually rules your life?
Who has the final word when obedience becomes inconvenient?
Whose approval matters most when faithfulness becomes costly?
There is a profound difference between defending Christianity as an identity and surrendering your life to Jesus as Lord.
You can win a political argument and still lose your tenderness toward people.
You can correctly identify governmental injustice and still be consumed by hatred.
You can quote Acts 5:29 and still refuse to obey the clear commands of Christ in your home.
You can defend the Bible loudly while ignoring what it says quietly.
And if that exposes something in your heart, do not run from the conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not simply a message about how Christians should respond to political authority.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is Lord.
And that announcement was never cheap.
When Jesus stood before Pontius Pilate, He faced a Roman governor who possessed real political power.
Pilate reminded Jesus of his authority to release Him or crucify Him.
Jesus answered:
“Thou wouldest have no power against me, except it were given thee from above.”
— John 19:11, American Standard Version (1901)
Think about that.
Jesus acknowledged that Pilate's authority was derivative.
It was not ultimate.
It existed under the sovereignty of God.
Yet Jesus did not pretend that Pilate's actions were morally innocent.
In that same verse, He spoke of sin and differing degrees of responsibility.
Political authority was real.
Moral accountability was also real.
And the Son of God stood before a human judge who did not fully understand Whom he was judging.
The One who formed the world was being questioned by a man whose next breath depended on the Creator's sustaining power.
The One who is perfectly righteous was about to be condemned.
The One who had committed no sin would be crucified.
And here is where everything changes.
Jesus did not go to the cross because earthly government was more powerful than He was.
He went willingly, in obedience to the Father's saving purpose, to give His life for sinners.
The cross exposed the injustice of human hearts.
But it also revealed the immeasurable mercy of God.
Human authorities condemned the innocent Christ.
And through His death and resurrection, God accomplished redemption for the guilty.
That is the scandal of the cross.
The Holy One suffered for sinners.
The righteous One bore our sins.
The rejected Savior became the hope of those who had rejected God.
And grace entered the very place where human wickedness seemed to have won.
Not because injustice is good.
Not because suffering is automatically holy.
Not because every ruler who harms someone is secretly carrying out God's moral will.
But because God is powerful enough to accomplish redemption even through the evil that human beings commit.
The cross never excuses the sin of those who condemned Jesus.
It reveals the mercy of the Savior who came to redeem sinners.

And if Christ could bring salvation through the darkest injustice in human history, then no believer needs to imagine that faithfulness has become meaningless simply because earthly power appears to be winning.
The resurrection declares otherwise.
Caesar does not have the final word.
Pilate does not have the final word.
The crowd does not have the final word.
The grave does not have the final word.
Jesus Christ does.
But we must also be honest about what that means.
The promise of Christ's victory does not guarantee that every faithful believer will escape imprisonment, persecution, poverty, or death in this life.
Some Christians have been delivered from danger.
Others have suffered terribly while remaining faithful.
The difference is not that one group possessed greater faith.
Our hope is not that obedience will always make us safe.
Our hope is that the risen Christ will never cease to be Lord, and that those who belong to Him have an inheritance that earthly rulers cannot destroy.
This is why the Christian response to government cannot be reduced to a slogan.
“Obey every command” is not the full teaching of Scripture.
“Resist every authority” is not the full teaching of Scripture either.
The biblical calling is deeper.
Submit to legitimate civil authority as an act of obedience to God.
Honor people without worshiping them.
Fulfill your responsibilities without surrendering your allegiance to Christ.
Pray for leaders, including those with whom you disagree.
Seek justice without surrendering to vengeance.
Refuse sin when any human authority demands it.
And when obedience becomes costly, remember the One who endured the cross and rose again.
Peter himself, the apostle who declared that God must be obeyed rather than men, later wrote:
“Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.”
— 1 Peter 2:17, American Standard Version (1901)
Four brief commands.
And notice the distinctions.
Honor everyone.
Love the family of believers.
Fear God.
Honor the king.
Peter does not say to fear the king as we fear God.
He reserves that ultimate reverence for the Lord.
In the original Greek, the contrast is equally clear:
τὸν θεὸν φοβεῖσθε, τὸν βασιλέα τιμᾶτε.
Ton theon phobeisthe, ton basilea timate.
“Fear God; honor the king.”
Not worship the king.
Not despise the king.
Honor him.
Fear God.
What a powerful correction for our generation.
We live in a world where political loyalty can become almost religious.
People defend leaders as though criticism were blasphemy.
Others despise leaders so deeply that they struggle to pray for them.
Families fracture.
Churches divide.
Christians begin measuring spiritual faithfulness by political affiliation rather than conformity to Jesus Christ.
And somewhere in the noise, the commands to love our neighbors, speak truth, practice humility, and make disciples are pushed aside.
But the church was never called to become the worshiping congregation of an earthly ruler.
Neither was it called to become a community held together by hatred of one.
The church belongs to Jesus Christ.
And His Kingdom is not confined to the rise and fall of governments.
So what should you do when a government command troubles your conscience?
First, make certain that your conscience is being instructed by Scripture rather than merely by fear, anger, political loyalty, or something you read online.
Ask what the law actually requires.
Ask whether it truly commands something God forbids or prohibits something God commands.
Study the relevant passages in context.
Seek counsel from mature believers who are willing to challenge you, not merely agree with you.
Distinguish between a command that is sinful and a policy that is inconvenient, unwise, or open to legitimate disagreement.
Where lawful avenues exist, use them responsibly.
And if a genuine conflict remains between obedience to God and obedience to human authority, remember that faithfulness to Christ comes first.
But do not forget that even righteous conviction must be expressed with integrity, wisdom, and love.
The manner of our witness matters.
The truth we defend must not become an excuse to abandon the character of the One who is Truth.
And perhaps the hardest command of all is this:
Pray for those who govern you.
Paul urges believers in 1 Timothy 2:1–2 to offer prayers and intercessions for all people, including kings and those in authority.
Not only the leaders we voted for.
Not only the officials who protect our interests.
Not only those who speak kindly about Christianity.
All who are in authority.
Pray for their repentance where they are wrong.
Pray for wisdom where they are confused.
Pray for justice where people are suffering.
Pray for restraint where power is being abused.
Pray for peace and for the freedom to live godly lives.
And pray that your own heart will not become so consumed by political anger that you forget the eternal destiny of the people you oppose.
Because Jesus died to save sinners.
Including sinners in positions of power.
Including sinners who have abused power and must be called to repentance and held accountable.
Including sinners who have spent their lives hating those in authority.
Including you.
Including me.
That is the part of the Gospel none of us can afford to forget.
We are not saved because we chose the correct political position.
We are not justified because we understood Romans 13 better than someone else.
We are not made righteous by our courage, patriotism, activism, or religious knowledge.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to repent.
To reject sin.
To pursue righteousness.
To love what God loves.
To stand for truth without becoming cruel.
To honor rightful authority without making an idol of it.
To remain faithful when compromise would be easier.
And to remember that our ultimate citizenship is in heaven, as Philippians 3:20 teaches.
Maybe you are reading this while feeling afraid of what is happening in your country.
Maybe you have watched corruption flourish and wondered whether God sees.
Maybe you have seen Scripture used to excuse injustice.
Maybe you have seen other Christians use God's name to justify hatred and rebellion.
Maybe you have been confused about what faithfulness actually requires.
Or maybe the deepest struggle is not with your government at all.
Maybe it is with the authority of Jesus over your own life.
You want Him as Savior, but you have resisted Him as Lord.
You want His protection, but you are afraid of what surrender might cost.
You want to stand courageously in public, but there is something hidden in private that you still refuse to bring into the light.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Jesus is not calling you to pretend that you are strong.
He is calling you to come to Him.
Bring your fear.
Bring your confusion.
Bring your political anger.
Bring your compromises.
Bring the sins you have excused and the wounds you have carried.
Confess what is wrong.
Turn from what is destroying your soul.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
The same Jesus who calls His people to costly obedience is the Jesus who gives grace to those who repent and believe.
You do not have to manufacture your own righteousness.
You need the righteousness and mercy of Christ.
And as you follow Him, you will discover that Christian courage is not the absence of fear.
It is faithfulness to Jesus even when fear is present.
Perhaps this article has unsettled you.
Perhaps it has challenged something you were taught.
Perhaps it has reminded you that the Christian life is far more serious than winning an argument about government.
If so, I would genuinely love to hear what God is teaching you.
Not to provoke another political fight.
Not to embarrass someone who disagrees.
But to invite a deeper conversation about Jesus Christ and the authority of His Word.
And if you have been blessed by this ministry and want to help us continue this work, I want to invite you into something more personal.
Not because you must support this particular ministry to prove that you love Jesus.
And certainly not because the grace of God can ever be purchased.

It can be part of your personal giving and stewardship, helping sustain the creation of Scripture-centered articles, devotionals, discipleship materials, and resources intended to encourage believers and introduce others to the hope found in Jesus Christ.
Paul reminds us in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
Without guilt.
Because the value of a gift is not measured merely by its amount, but by the willing heart from which it comes.
These free resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, grow in biblical understanding, and develop a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
Our desire is not simply to produce content that people read once and forget.
It is to help cultivate a community that reads God's Word, tests teachings against Scripture, prays faithfully, encourages one another, and grows in obedience to Christ.
A comment can open a conversation that another struggling believer desperately needs.
A prayer can express your dependence on the God who alone brings lasting spiritual fruit.
We do not know every heart that these messages may reach.
But we know whom we are called to proclaim.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord over all.
And now, before you leave, I want to bring you back to that courtroom where we began.
The judge is still waiting.
The threat is still real.
The pressure to compromise has not disappeared.
And the question remains.
Would Romans 13 require you to deny Jesus simply because someone in authority commanded it?
No.
The same God who calls you to respect legitimate earthly authority commands your ultimate allegiance to His Son.
You may honor the ruler.
You may fulfill your civic duties.
You may submit to laws that do not require you to sin.
You may pray for the very official who mistreats you.
But you must never give to an earthly authority the worship, loyalty, and obedience that belong to God alone.
And if faithfulness becomes costly, remember this:
The Savior you follow once stood before an earthly governor.
He was condemned though He was innocent.
He was crucified though He was righteous.
He was buried though He was the Author of life.
But on the third day, He rose.
And today, the One who stood before Pilate reigns above every earthly throne.
His Kingdom will not be overturned by an election.
His truth will not be erased by a decree.
His resurrection will not be undone by a prison sentence.
His grace is sufficient for repentant sinners.
And His promise of eternal life cannot be revoked by Caesar.
So honor those who govern.
Pray for those who lead.
Obey what is right.
Refuse what God forbids.
Love your enemies.
Guard your conscience with Scripture.
And follow Jesus Christ above all.
Because when every earthly throne has fallen silent, one King will still reign.
Never surrender to Caesar what Christ purchased with His blood.
